newsitem.title: CHINA: China wants foreign gold investors despite problems.
newsitem.headline: China wants foreign gold investors despite problems.

text.p: China is determined to woo foreign funds to its gold industry despite difficulties that have deterred potential investors since Beijing opened the closely guarded sector three years ago, state media said on Sunday.

"You cannot expect everything to change in a short period of time," the China Daily Business Weekly quoted Ai Dacheng, deputy director of the gold bureau under the Ministry of Metallurgical Industry, as saying.

Among problems keeping away foreign investors was the fact that China's gold sector remained under central control, missing out on market-oriented economic reforms in many other areas of China's economy.
"During the long opening process, China needs understanding from the foreign partners since the management of the industry is still a planned one," Ai said.
"China needs to work out a series of regulations that suit both the domestic situation and international practice," he said.
China decided to open low-grade gold mines to foreign partners on a trial basis in August 1993 and last May agreed to allow foreign firms to conduct risk prospecting in central and western China.
One difficulty foreign investors faced was procedures that required them to go through many different departments to set up their investment, Ai said.
Several projects had been submitted for approval, he said.
He cited Canada's Asia Minerals Corp which is in talks on a 50-50 joint venture with the Zhaoyuan Gold Group in eastern Shandong province, one of China's major gold-producing areas.
The project, with proven reserves of 70 tonnes of gold, was nearing final approval, Ai said.

In southwestern Guizhou province, Australia's Broken Hill Proprietary Ltd, Gencor Group of South Africa and Newmont China Ltd of the United States were all interested in cooperating with the local government in the Lannigou gold mine. The mine had proven reserves of 60 tonnes, he said.
Results of the projects were expected in five months, he said.

In southwestern Guangxi, a potential project between an unidentified Canadian firm and the local gold bureau in Baise prefecture had been submitted to the State Economic and Trade Commission for approval, he said.
China produced 120.6 tonnes of gold last year, up from 108 tonnes in 1995.
